sources.description: A historical study written in 1949 and published in 1981. Quigley traces elite networks through education, publishing, imperial governance and foreign policy. His appendix labels the membership roster tentative, with possible errors and explicitly bracketed conjectures. The archive distinguishes reported roles from his inferred affiliations. The PDF remains a local research document and is not redistributed by this site.

sources.title: The State, the Deep State, and the Wall Street Overworld
sources.author: Peter Dale Scott
sources.description: An Asia-Pacific Journal / Japan Focus article examining the interplay of security institutions, financial elites and international covert operations. Causal arguments and quoted interpretations are attributed to Scott or their named authors; the notes include denials and evidentiary qualifications. The PDF header gives March 3, the recommended citation March 10, and the revision March 13, 2014.
sources.coverage: Article and all endnotes reviewed. Selective extraction of dated events, institutions and people; passing names are not exhaustive.

evidenceIssues.description: Publication header and recommended citation disagree (March 3 versus March 10); explicit update March 13, 2014.
Scott notes establishment writers describe Copeland memoirs as unreliable; claims from Copeland remain attributed.
Nixon briefcase donation story is disputed by Kolb, and Baer gives 1968 rather than 1972; not included as a factual dated event.
Safari Club resort and intelligence alliance are separate entities; Scott presents both official-policy origin and later circumvention interpretations.
Notes 103 and 105 explicitly state no published evidence Copeland was involved in Safari Club covert operations; no membership edge created.
Scott’s oil-boycott interpretation is denied by Exxon corporate history in note 48.
The article’s parenthetical company labels conflate Standard Oil of New York/Socony and California. A collective oil-cartel record avoids reproducing the naming error.
Ownership and job descriptions are historical statements as of the 2014 article, not claims about current roles.

sources.title: The Yankee and Cowboy War
sources.author: Carl Oglesby
sources.subtitle: Conspiracies from Dallas to Watergate
sources.description: Oglesby interprets Dallas, Watergate and the Hughes business struggle through competing elite factions. Yankee and Cowboy are his analytical labels, not verified formal organizations. Alternative assassination, covert-operation and sabotage theories remain source-attributed; denials and official accounts are preserved.
sources.coverage: Selected records across the narrative, 1977 preface and appendix, with notes and index used as finding aids. The scan contains OCR errors; names and dates are normalized cautiously. This is an attributed digest, not an exhaustive extraction of every reference.

sourceSummaries.summary: Roberts says an April 1967 insurance dispute first drew him into conflicts with local officials. He reports winning his case but later discovering that insurance companies had paid the claimant anyway. He interprets the handling of his complaint as part of the same system he later alleges around Alioto.
details: In his letter to Nader, Roberts recalls a woman jumping in front of his car and characterizes the incident as an attempted insurance fraud. He says he defeated the case, then learned that a group of insurers had nevertheless paid her. The passage gives his account; it does not reproduce the judgment or payment records.

Roberts says he took the matter to Police Chief Cahill and that his material was buried. He connects this episode to what he describes as decades of cooperation among insurance companies, corporations and officials. Immediately afterward he contrasts this political involvement with his previous years of mineral experimentation and voluntary isolation.
sourceSummaries.context: This is the earliest dated personal grievance in the extracted sequence. Roberts presents it as the background to his later collision, requests for lawyers and broad conspiracy allegations.
sourceSummaries.precisionNote: The source specifies April 1967, not a day; the month is plotted from April 1.

events.name: Roberts reports an Alioto-family collision
events.description: Roberts reports that a member of the Alioto family hit his car at Franklin and Lombard Streets in San Francisco on September 16, 1968. He says the incident was covered up and a report filed under Kathryn Hollister’s name. For him, that alleged concealment becomes the central link between local politics, Nixon’s election and Chappaquiddick.

sourceSummaries.summary: Rhodes’s 1875 Confession of Faith imagined an imperial brotherhood recruiting capable people and using their combined resources to extend British power. details: Rhodes proposed a body modeled on the Jesuits, organized around service to the British Empire rather than religious conversion. Its potential recruits included talented students, wealthy men lacking a purpose, younger sons without opportunities, and people frustrated by existing political institutions. Ability, character and shared commitment mattered more than personal reward.

Quigley connects this statement to the first five wills, which explicitly referred to a secret society, and to the later scholarship provisions. His claim is that the educational bequest continued the earlier political purpose. That continuity is his interpretation of Rhodes’s changing testamentary arrangements, rather than something established by the scholarship institution alone.
sourceSummaries.context: This begins the thread connecting imperial ideology, recruitment, philanthropy and the later Rhodes Trust.

details: The proposed objectives went beyond acquiring territory. Rhodes wanted British emigration and settlement, colonial representation in an imperial parliament, and a consolidated power large enough to prevent future wars. The association was to follow a Jesuit-style organizational model. Quigley traces successive changes of trustees through Rhodes’s later wills, explaining that the eventual scholarship trustees were part of this longer evolution. The passage establishes the early wording and custodians of the plan; Quigley’s larger argument is that later public institutions did not replace its political ambitions.

details: John Morley edited the newspaper while Stead served as assistant editor, becoming editor in 1883. Quigley suggests Goschen’s influence helped Milner enter journalism, but presents that causal step as probable rather than documented certainty. The importance of this episode is the formation of personal ties: newspaper employment connected people who later operated in government, colonial administration and publicity. The trip intersects the Commonwealth consultation and India reform threads through Curtis’s changing political ideas.
details: The immediate question was whether a self-governing South Africa might refuse participation in a future war it had not helped decide. The visitors sought Canadian experience with imperial relations. During a walk in the Rockies, Marris argued that self-government was the only intelligible long-term objective of British policy in India.

Curtis later identified the conversation as a milestone, moving from a conception of self-government as specifically Western to a principle applicable to all peoples. After returning to South Africa he drafted an imperial-relations memorandum, then sailed to New Zealand to organize study groups. Quigley links the tour both to the Round Table’s expansion and to the intellectual origins of Indian constitutional reform.

Quigley argues that Brand engineered the transaction, securing ownership after the network’s editorial influence had proved vulnerable to a proprietor’s opposition. This connects business ownership, Dawson’s editorship, Brand’s career and the newspaper’s later foreign-policy role.

details: Dawson had left in 1919 after a dispute with Northcliffe. With the acquisition, Colonel John Jacob Astor became chairman of the publishing company and Brand served on its board. Waldorf Astor’s family and social connections overlapped with Brand’s: the men had attended New College and married sisters.

Quigley distinguishes ownership from the broader center of the network, which he locates increasingly at All Souls rather than the newspaper alone. The purchase nevertheless provided an enduring institutional base for editorial appointments and policy campaigns. His claim of coordinated control is an interpretation of the financial transaction and overlapping personnel, especially consequential in the period before Munich.

The event is important because the network’s activities did not depend on Milner holding a ministry. Personal relationships and institutional positions supplied continuity while the original leader disappeared from public affairs.

The conference joins international-affairs institutes, Pacific Relations contacts and practical Commonwealth consultation.
details: Forty-three delegates and thirty-three secretaries attended, with Carnegie money covering travel. The initiative developed through earlier Institute of Pacific Relations meetings; a Cecil-led committee prepared the agenda at Chatham House. Macadam headed the conference secretariat, while Hodson and George Parkin Glazebrook served national delegations.

The recommendations included diplomatic status for Dominion High Commissioners, training in London, exchanged representatives, tribunals for disputes, support for collective security and American cooperation. Proceedings edited by Toynbee shortened remarks and did not name speakers. Quigley argues that prominent chairmanships and secretarial posts gave his circle influence greater than its minority share of delegates.

This connects imperial constitutional arguments, Coupland’s academic-policy role and the Palestine mandate controversy.

Ormsby-Gore carried the proposal through a White Paper and defended it before the League’s Mandates Commission; Lugard, Lang and Amery supported it publicly. Quigley infers that Coupland may have discussed the change with the inner circle after returning to England. This is not a recorded meeting or established drafting instruction. The subsequent Woodhead inquiry rejected partition as impractical, so the event records a proposed policy and its advocacy rather than a partition actually carried out.

details: At Robert Cecil’s suggestion, General Tasker Bliss chaired the joint meeting. Quigley identifies Curtis as the decisive founder and argues that the British experts largely came from his Milner and Cecil circles. He similarly emphasizes Morgan-connected American participants. The conference is the specific institutional bridge; the claim that the resulting institutes extended a coordinated financial and political network is the author’s interpretation of the personnel and funding.

details: The former Kinnaird house had once been occupied by William Pitt, supplying the name Chatham House. Leonard required the institute to raise an endowment yielding at least £10,000 annually. Treasurer John Power gave another £10,000 for an assembly hall, while Edith Lyttelton supervised renovation and furnishing.

A group led by A. F. Pollard opposed accepting the gift because of its continuing costs. Quigley says Curtis mobilized supporters to defeat that opposition, citing a Dove letter to Brand. The account makes the organizational issue specific: securing a permanent headquarters involved fundraising and internal governance, not simply receiving a building without obligations.

details: The early sequence continued at Honolulu in 1927, Kyoto in 1929, Shanghai in 1931, Banff in 1933 and Yosemite in 1936. Eggleston presided over many early meetings. The endowment joins the South African, Round Table and RIIA threads through a recurring source of finance.

He later returns to the Italian election while discussing Saudi-financed payments and argues that unconventional financial channels survived subsequent legal reforms. details: The work included general advice to the Egyptian government and assistance to a private textile mill. Its relevance to a Quigley overlay is that Churchill also appears in Quigley’s historical account—not that Quigley endorses Roberts’ story.
